turns.note: Initial seven-column flowsheet: keep ethane as a minor impurity in the C3 blend, recover C4/C5 blends, C6 paraffin and naphthene blends, and pure heptane, octane, and nonane. Moderate staging and reflux establish converged baselines and reveal where purity or cost needs adjustment.
Reset to one convergent feed column and sharpen the C5/C6 cut; this is the key split for recovering the C3, C4, C5 and C6 blend values downstream.
Copy the measured convergent revenue-generating flowsheet and remove two downstream columns whose measured outlets had zero sales value, preserving the C3 and C5 blend products while cutting cost.
Copy the measured 1.088 design. I am testing two high-value additions: a C6 paraffin/naphthene split on BT and an octane/nonane split on BBBB; both outlets have potential blend or pure-product sales.

Copy the measured 1.088 six-column design. I am testing a heavier C6 paraffin/naphthene cut, C3/C4 recovery, and a two-step C6-naphthene/C7/C8 sequence; these target large unsold streams while retaining all current sales.

I am sharpening the three largest remaining recovery opportunities: C6 paraffins/naphthenes, the C4 blend, and octane/nonane. Their measured outlets are currently just below sale purity or remain completely mixed, so the potential revenue gain should justify more severe columns.

Measured unsold pools contain valuable C4, C6/naphthalene, C7/C8, and cyclohexane/C7 mixtures. I am adding targeted splits for those pools and sharpening the two octane-producing columns to seek premium-grade sales.

Interpretation: the measured zero-value C6 naphthene, C7/C8, and C8/C9 pools are close to valuable binary cuts, so I am sharpening those columns. I am also driving residual butane overhead in TTBB to recover a C4 blend rather than an unsold butane/pentane bottoms.

The measured flowsheet has several high-flow unsold outlets. I am adding small polishing columns for C4/C5, octane and cyclohexane recovery, while sharpening the difficult C6 paraffin/naphthene split to convert its two zero-value outlets into blends.

I am testing a much sharper C6 paraffin/naphthene cut because both current outlets are unsold despite substantial blend value, and a modestly sharper C7/C8 cut to try for premium octane. I am also deleting the cyclohexane polishing column whose measured outlets are both worthless.

Measured losses are concentrated in the naphthene outlet and several nearly binary residual streams. I am testing lower pressure for the difficult hexane/MCP split and sharper small-column cuts, while removing the TTBBB polishing column if the improved parent split makes both outlets saleable.

The measured zero-value leaves still contain valuable, separable components. I am adding five small recovery columns: n-butane from TTBBB, cyclohexane from BBTTTT, octane from BBTBBT, octane/nonane from BBBBTB, and a hexane/naphthene cut on BTBB; the first four should be low-cost incremental upgrades, while BTBB targets a much larger C6 naphthene blend sale.

The measured C5 blend is worth $645M/yr versus roughly $920M/yr if both pentanes reach premium purity, so I am testing a dedicated C5 splitter. I am also moving the BTBB cut from methylcyclopentane/cyclohexane toward hexane/naphthenes, and deleting the measured zero-value BBTTTT polishing column.
Sell the already blend-grade C5 stream directly, remove the invalid and valueless naphthene split, and retain only the profitable C6-paraffin recovery with a cheaper BTB column.

Prune the measured zero-value C6 bottoms split and reduce its parent severity while retaining the valuable C6 paraffin blend. Also test whether one sharper propane/C4 column can replace the two-column light-end tail.
The expanded 20-column tree is substantially below the recorded best, so I am restoring the best valid design before making any further targeted changes.

Measured facts: six currently unsold outlets contain valuable binary or near-binary mixtures, while the prior convergent sequence shows that small downstream columns are inexpensive. Interpretation: one additional sharp split on each outlet should recover cyclohexane, heptane, octane, nonane, propane/isobutane, and C4/C5 value at high marginal profit.
The current BBB tops are 97% octane and sell for $480.4M/yr; I am testing a sharper C8/C9 cut to reach the 99% premium while preserving the downstream nonane recovery.

Target the two near-premium heavy products: BBBT is 96% octane and BBBBB 96% nonane, so sharper splits could earn the 20% premium. Simultaneously test whether the very expensive BTB column can be moderated while retaining its two saleable outlets.

The current 30-column design is less profitable than the saved best because several tiny terminal separations add cost without sales. I am restoring the measured best design before making targeted cost reductions.

The measured plant has several small columns with one saleable outlet and one zero-value outlet. I am sharpening only those inexpensive polishers to recover isobutane, butane, cyclohexane and nonane sales while leaving the large profitable separations unchanged.

The measured BTB cut has sale-quality outlets with some purity slack but is the plant's most expensive small column. I am testing a modest reduction in stages and reflux/boil-up to trade a little purity for lower annual cost; only BTB and its downstream child should need new solves.
The measured BBBT octane stream is already 97% pure and worth $480.4M/yr; I am sharpening only this cut to target the 99% premium while preserving its converged pressure.
The measured octane tops stream is 97% pure, just below premium grade. I am modestly increasing separation severity to capture the 20% octane price uplift while retaining the converged flowsheet.
The current 30-column design measures 3.229, below the recorded best of 3.267. With only two solves remaining, I am restoring the best valid design rather than risking an unvalidated final change.

The measured BTBBT stream contains about 64 mol/s methylcyclopentane but is unsold because of n-hexane contamination. I am testing a much sharper leaf-column split to recover that pure product while retaining the measured saleable naphthene bottoms; this is a hypothesis, and only this leaf column needs a new solve.
With only one solve left, restore the best measured valid design (reward 3.267) rather than risk a new unproven column setting; the current fully converged design is slightly lower at 3.254.

Use the final solve on the largest unsold leaf pool: BTBBT contains about 64 mol/s methylcyclopentane and 34 mol/s n-hexane. A sharp low-pressure hexane/MCP split could convert both into premium products, with modest diameter cost at this small flow.
